newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end mixed ahead of July jobs data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end mixed ahead of July jobs data.

text.p: U.S. stocks put in a mixed performance on Thursday, with investors taking a cautious tack ahead of a potentially market-moving report on U.S. employment in July.
The Dow industrials snapped a streak of three consecutive record closing highs, ending down about 32 points at 8223.
But the broader market was firm. Continued strength in market-leading computer and financial stocks pushed the Standard & Poor's 500 and the Nasdaq composite to fresh highs.
The S&P 500 rose about two points to 954, and the Nasdaq composite finished up six to 1594.
On the New York Stock Exchange, advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 17-to-11 ratio.
Market players linked the Dow drop to profit-taking by investors wary of a report on July U.S. payrolls, wages and employment, due ahead of the stock market's opening Friday.
"I think the lack of enthusiasm is because of waiting for tomorrow morning's release," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers.

Economists on average expect the report to show the economy created 193,000 new jobs in July, compared with 217,000 in June. The unemployment rate is expected to dip to 4.9 percent from 5.0 percent in June.
The market is also awaiting the July report from the National Association of Purchasing Management on Friday.

Stronger-than-expected data could potentially derail the rally in stocks and bonds by raising inflation fears. But some analysts said the recent wave of economic news showing mild growth and subdued inflation reduced the chances the market will be blindsided by the reports.

"These things weigh a lot less on our minds now that there's such a preponderance of evidence that the economy's growing at a strong rate without inflation pressure," said Robert Robbins, market strategist at Robinson-Humphrey Co.

On Thursday the government reported that the gross domestic product expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the April-June second quarter, less than half the revised 4.9 percent pace in the first quarter.
Meanwhile, a key inflation measure in the GDP report -- the implicit price deflator -- edged up at a 1.4 percent rate in the second quarter after a 2.4 percent first-quarter rise.
The inflation-sensitive bond market extended its rally, with the 30-year Treasury up 13/32 in late trade, its yield dropping to 6.30 percent.

Interest-rate senstive stocks, including banks and brokerages, were among strongest performers. Chase Manhattan Corp rose 1-1/16 to 113-9/16 and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co gained 2-11/16 to 52-7/16.

Some traders said they saw investors shifting to stocks that can produce consistent earnings in a slowing economy. Schering-Plough Corp, a drug company, rose 3-1/16 to 54-9/16, and Campbell Soup Co added 3/16 to 51-14/16.

"I'm seeing some profit-taking, moving away from the real growth stocks and into more defensive issues," said Frank Calta, managing director of institutional trading at Dain Bosworth. "It will be interesting to see if this pattern continues over the next couple of weeks."

Personal computer stocks extended their strong performance. Dell Computer Corp rose 3-1/4 to 85-1/2 after Morgan Stanley Dean Witter raised its 1997 and 1998 earnings estimates on Dell. Compaq Computer Corp gained 2-1/8 to 57-1/8, and Hewlett-Packard Co added 2-3/16 to 70.

Student Loan Marketing Association, known as Sallie Mae, ended up 4-13/16 to 149-15/16 after shareholders voted to privatize the government-sponsored enterprise through a plan put forward by a dissident group.

Fast-food chain Wendy's International Inc fell 2-13/16 to 24-1/2. Analysts at Smith Barney and Merrill Lynch downgraded the stock after it reported quarterly earnings and said it faced difficult second-half sales comparisons, with a higher tax rate and rising costs of labor and raw materials.
The S&P 500 rose two points to 954.29, a record. The Nasdaq Composite rose 5.76 points to 1593.81, a record.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
